title: 03. Multiprocessing: Multiprocessing Communication
summary: Covers Inter-Process Communication (IPC) Overview, Queues, Pipes, Managers, Shared Memory (Value and Array).

diagrams.title: Choosing an IPC mechanism
diagrams.mermaid:
flowchart TD
  need["Processes need to exchange data"] --> q{"Shape of the communication?"}
  q -->|"many producers / consumers"| queue["Queue — pickled messages, process-safe"]
  q -->|"exactly two endpoints"| pipe["Pipe — faster, two connection objects"]
  q -->|"shared dict or list"| mgr["Manager — proxies to a server process, flexible but slow"]
  q -->|"numbers or arrays, hot path"| shm["Value / Array / shared_memory — no copying, you add locking"]
diagrams.explain: Every mechanism trades convenience against speed. Queues and pipes **copy** data by pickling; managers add a network-style round trip per operation; shared memory avoids copying but leaves synchronisation to you. Start with a Queue and move to shared memory only for large numeric data on a hot path.

sections.title: 6.2 Queues
sections.body:
**What this code covers**

- Produce items and put them in queue
- Consume items from queue
- Produce items
- Consume items until done event is set and queue is empty
- Non-blocking get with timeout
- Shared queue and event
- Signal consumers to finish
- Mark task as done

**Defines:** `producer()`, `consumer()`, `worker()`

### Visual Explanation


### Queue Types

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                         QUEUE TYPES                                          │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                              │
│  1. Queue (multiprocessing.Queue)                                            │
│     ────────────────────────────────                                         │
│     • Full-featured, FIFO queue                                              │
│     • Supports qsize(), empty(), full()                                      │
│     • Has background thread for writing                                      │
│     • Needs close() and join_thread() for cleanup                            │
│                                                                              │
│  2. SimpleQueue (multiprocessing.SimpleQueue)                                │
│     ────────────────────────────────────────────                             │
│     • Simpler, more reliable                                                 │
│     • No qsize(), empty(), full()                                            │
│     • No close() needed                                                      │
│     • Slightly faster                                                        │
│                                                                              │
│  3. JoinableQueue (multiprocessing.JoinableQueue)                            │
│     ────────────────────────────────────────────────                         │
│     • Like Queue but supports task_done() and join()                         │
│     • Producer can wait until consumers finish all items                     │
│     • Ideal for task tracking                                                │
│                                                                              │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

### Code Examples

#### Example 1: Basic Queue Usage

```python
import multiprocessing
import time
import random

def producer(queue, items):
    """Produce items and put them in queue"""
    for item in items:
        print(f"[Producer] Producing: {item}")
        queue.put(item)
        time.sleep(random.uniform(0.1, 0.3))

    # Signal done
    queue.put(None)  # Sentinel value
    print("[Producer] Done!")

def consumer(queue):
    """Consume items from queue"""
    while True:
        item = queue.get()
        if item is None:  # Sentinel received
            print("[Consumer] Received sentinel, stopping")
            break

        print(f"[Consumer] Processing: {item}")
        time.sleep(random.uniform(0.2, 0.4))

    print("[Consumer] Done!")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Create queue
    queue = multiprocessing.Queue()

    # Create processes
    items = ['apple', 'banana', 'cherry', 'date', 'elderberry']

    producer_proc = multiprocessing.Process(target=producer, args=(queue, items))
    consumer_proc = multiprocessing.Process(target=consumer, args=(queue,))

    # Start
    producer_proc.start()
    consumer_proc.start()

    # Wait
    producer_proc.join()
    consumer_proc.join()

    print("All done!")
```

#### Example 2: Multiple Producers and Consumers

```python
import multiprocessing
import time
import random

def producer(queue, producer_id, num_items):
    """Produce items"""
    for i in range(num_items):
        item = f"P{producer_id}-Item{i}"
        queue.put(item)
        print(f"[Producer {producer_id}] Produced: {item}")
        time.sleep(random.uniform(0.05, 0.15))

def consumer(queue, consumer_id, done_event):
    """Consume items until done event is set and queue is empty"""
    processed = 0
    while True:
        try:
            # Non-blocking get with timeout
            item = queue.get(timeout=0.5)
            print(f"[Consumer {consumer_id}] Processed: {item}")
            processed += 1
            time.sleep(random.uniform(0.1, 0.2))
        except multiprocessing.queues.Empty:
            if done_event.is_set():
                break

    print(f"[Consumer {consumer_id}] Finished. Processed {processed} items.")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Shared queue and event
    queue = multiprocessing.Queue()
    done_event = multiprocessing.Event()

    # Create producers
    producers = []
    for i in range(3):
        p = multiprocessing.Process(target=producer, args=(queue, i, 5))
        producers.append(p)

    # Create consumers
    consumers = []
    for i in range(2):
        c = multiprocessing.Process(target=consumer, args=(queue, i, done_event))
        consumers.append(c)

    # Start all
    for p in producers:
        p.start()
    for c in consumers:
        c.start()

    # Wait for producers
    for p in producers:
        p.join()

    # Signal consumers to finish
    done_event.set()

    # Wait for consumers
    for c in consumers:
        c.join()

    print("All done!")
```

#### Example 3: JoinableQueue with Task Tracking

```python
import multiprocessing
import time
import random

def worker(queue, worker_id):
    """Process tasks from joinable queue"""
    while True:
        try:
            task = queue.get(timeout=1.0)
        except:
            break

        print(f"[Worker {worker_id}] Processing task: {task}")
        time.sleep(random.uniform(0.2, 0.5))  # Simulate work

        # Mark task as done
        queue.task_done()
        print(f"[Worker {worker_id}] Completed task: {task}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Create joinable queue
    queue = multiprocessing.JoinableQueue()

    # Create workers
    workers = []
    for i in range(3):
        w = multiprocessing.Process(target=worker, args=(queue, i))
        w.daemon = True
        w.start()
        workers.append(w)

    # Add tasks
    tasks = [f"Task-{i}" for i in range(10)]
    for task in tasks:
        queue.put(task)

    print("[Main] All tasks submitted. Waiting for completion...")

    # Wait for all tasks to be processed
    queue.join()  # Blocks until all task_done() called

    print("[Main] All tasks completed!")
```

diagrams.title: What happens inside multiprocessing.Queue.put()
diagrams.mermaid:
sequenceDiagram
  participant P as Producer process
  participant F as Feeder thread
  participant OS as OS pipe
  participant C as Consumer process
  P->>F: put(obj) returns quickly
  F->>F: pickle obj
  F->>OS: write bytes
  C->>OS: get() reads bytes
  C->>C: unpickle into a new object
diagrams.explain: `put()` hands the object to a background feeder thread that pickles it and writes it to an OS pipe; the consumer unpickles a **copy**. So mutating the object after sending it does not affect what the consumer sees, and every object you send must be picklable — lambdas, open sockets and locks are not.

sections.title: 6.3 Pipes
sections.body:
**What this code covers**

- Send messages through pipe
- Receive messages from pipe
- Play ping-pong through pipe
- Server that responds to requests
- Create pipe - returns two Connection objects

**Defines:** `sender()`, `receiver()`, `player()`, `server()`, `client()`

### Visual Explanation

```
╔════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
║                           PIPES                                             ║
╠════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╣
║                                                                             ║
║  Pipe creates TWO connection objects:                                       ║
║                                                                             ║
║  DUPLEX=True (default):                                                     ║
║  ─────────────────────                                                      ║
║                                                                             ║
║  ┌────────────────────┐                      ┌────────────────────┐        ║
║  │     Process A      │                      │     Process B      │        ║
║  │                    │                      │                    │        ║
║  │  ┌──────────────┐  │                      │  ┌──────────────┐  │        ║
║  │  │ Connection 1 │  │                      │  │ Connection 2 │  │        ║
║  │  │              │  │                      │  │              │  │        ║
║  │  │   .send() ───┼──┼─────────────────────►┼──┼─►.recv()     │  │        ║
║  │  │              │  │                      │  │              │  │        ║
║  │  │   .recv() ◄──┼──┼◄─────────────────────┼──┼───.send()    │  │        ║
║  │  │              │  │                      │  │              │  │        ║
║  │  └──────────────┘  │                      │  └──────────────┘  │        ║
║  └────────────────────┘                      └────────────────────┘        ║
║                                                                             ║
║  DUPLEX=False (one-way):                                                    ║
║  ───────────────────────                                                    ║
║                                                                             ║
║  ┌────────────────────┐                      ┌────────────────────┐        ║
║  │     Process A      │                      │     Process B      │        ║
║  │  ┌──────────────┐  │                      │  ┌──────────────┐  │        ║
║  │  │ Connection 1 │  │                      │  │ Connection 2 │  │        ║
║  │  │  (receive)   │  │                      │  │   (send)     │  │        ║
║  │  │   .recv() ◄──┼──┼◄─────────────────────┼──┼───.send()    │  │        ║
║  │  └──────────────┘  │                      │  └──────────────┘  │        ║
║  └────────────────────┘                      └────────────────────┘        ║
║                                                                             ║
╚════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝
```

### Code Examples

#### Example 1: Simple Pipe Communication

```python
import multiprocessing
import time

def sender(conn):
    """Send messages through pipe"""
    messages = ["Hello", "World", "From", "Process"]

    for msg in messages:
        print(f"[Sender] Sending: {msg}")
        conn.send(msg)
        time.sleep(0.5)

    conn.send(None)  # Signal done
    conn.close()

def receiver(conn):
    """Receive messages from pipe"""
    while True:
        msg = conn.recv()
        if msg is None:
            print("[Receiver] Received end signal")
            break
        print(f"[Receiver] Received: {msg}")

    conn.close()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Create pipe - returns two Connection objects
    parent_conn, child_conn = multiprocessing.Pipe()

    # Create processes
    p1 = multiprocessing.Process(target=sender, args=(parent_conn,))
    p2 = multiprocessing.Process(target=receiver, args=(child_conn,))

    p1.start()
    p2.start()

    p1.join()
    p2.join()

    print("Done!")
```

#### Example 2: Bidirectional Ping-Pong

```python
import multiprocessing
import time

def player(conn, name, start_first=False):
    """Play ping-pong through pipe"""

    if start_first:
        print(f"[{name}] Starting with PING")
        conn.send("PING")

    for _ in range(5):
        msg = conn.recv()
        print(f"[{name}] Received: {msg}")

        time.sleep(0.3)

        # Reply with opposite
        response = "PONG" if msg == "PING" else "PING"
        print(f"[{name}] Sending: {response}")
        conn.send(response)

    conn.close()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Create bidirectional pipe
    conn1, conn2 = multiprocessing.Pipe(duplex=True)

    p1 = multiprocessing.Process(target=player, args=(conn1, "Player1", True))
    p2 = multiprocessing.Process(target=player, args=(conn2, "Player2", False))

    p1.start()
    p2.start()

    p1.join()
    p2.join()
```

#### Example 3: Client-Server Pattern

```python
import multiprocessing
import time
import random

def server(conn):
    """Server that responds to requests"""
    print("[Server] Starting...")

    while True:
        # Receive request
        request = conn.recv()

        if request is None:
            print("[Server] Shutdown request received")
            break

        command, data = request
        print(f"[Server] Received command: {command}, data: {data}")

        # Process request
        if command == "SQUARE":
            result = data ** 2
        elif command == "DOUBLE":
            result = data * 2
        elif command == "REVERSE":
            result = data[::-1] if isinstance(data, str) else list(reversed(data))
        else:
            result = {"error": "Unknown command"}

        # Send response
        conn.send(result)
        print(f"[Server] Sent result: {result}")

    conn.close()
    print("[Server] Shutdown complete")

def client(conn):
    """Client that sends requests"""
    print("[Client] Starting...")

    requests = [
        ("SQUARE", 7),
        ("DOUBLE", 21),
        ("REVERSE", "Hello"),
        ("SQUARE", 100),
    ]

    for cmd, data in requests:
        print(f"[Client] Sending request: {cmd}({data})")
        conn.send((cmd, data))

        response = conn.recv()
        print(f"[Client] Received response: {response}")
        time.sleep(0.5)

    # Shutdown server
    conn.send(None)
    conn.close()
    print("[Client] Done")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    server_conn, client_conn = multiprocessing.Pipe()

    server_proc = multiprocessing.Process(target=server, args=(server_conn,))
    client_proc = multiprocessing.Process(target=client, args=(client_conn,))

    server_proc.start()
    client_proc.start()

    client_proc.join()
    server_proc.join()
```

sections.title: 6.4 Managers
sections.body:
**What this code covers**

- Worker that updates shared dictionary
- Increment counter in shared namespace
- Update status in shared namespace
- Collect data samples and add to shared list
- Create manager and shared dictionary
- Calculate statistics per collector

**Defines:** `worker()`, `counter_process()`, `status_process()`, `data_collector()`

### Visual Explanation

```
╔════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
║                           MANAGER                                           ║
╠════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╣
║                                                                             ║
║  Manager creates a server process that holds the real data:                 ║
║                                                                             ║
```

### Manager Types

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                     MANAGER SHARED TYPES                                     │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                              │
│  manager = multiprocessing.Manager()                                         │
│                                                                              │
│  • manager.list()       → Shared list                                        │
│  • manager.dict()       → Shared dictionary                                  │
│  • manager.Namespace()  → Shared namespace (attribute access)                │
│  • manager.Queue()      → Shared queue                                       │
│  • manager.Event()      → Shared event                                       │
│  • manager.Lock()       → Shared lock                                        │
│  • manager.Semaphore()  → Shared semaphore                                   │
│  • manager.Condition()  → Shared condition                                   │
│  • manager.Barrier()    → Shared barrier                                     │
│  • manager.Value()      → Shared value                                       │
│  • manager.Array()      → Shared array                                       │
│                                                                              │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

### Code Examples

#### Example 1: Shared Dictionary

```python
import multiprocessing
import time
import random

def worker(shared_dict, worker_id, num_items):
    """Worker that updates shared dictionary"""
    for i in range(num_items):
        key = f"worker_{worker_id}_item_{i}"
        value = random.randint(1, 100)

        shared_dict[key] = value
        print(f"[Worker {worker_id}] Set {key} = {value}")

        time.sleep(random.uniform(0.1, 0.3))

    print(f"[Worker {worker_id}] Done. Dict size: {len(shared_dict)}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Create manager and shared dictionary
    with multiprocessing.Manager() as manager:
        shared_dict = manager.dict()

        # Create workers
        workers = []
        for i in range(3):
            p = multiprocessing.Process(
                target=worker,
                args=(shared_dict, i, 4)
            )
            workers.append(p)
            p.start()

        # Wait for all
        for p in workers:
            p.join()

        # Show final dictionary
        print(f"\nFinal dictionary ({len(shared_dict)} items):")
        for key, value in sorted(shared_dict.items()):
            print(f"  {key}: {value}")
```

#### Example 2: Shared Namespace

```python
import multiprocessing
import time

def counter_process(namespace, lock):
    """Increment counter in shared namespace"""
    for _ in range(1000):
        with lock:
            namespace.counter += 1

def status_process(namespace, lock):
    """Update status in shared namespace"""
    for status in ["starting", "running", "processing", "complete"]:
        with lock:
            namespace.status = status
            namespace.update_count += 1
        time.sleep(0.5)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    with multiprocessing.Manager() as manager:
        # Create shared namespace
        ns = manager.Namespace()
        ns.counter = 0
        ns.status = "initialized"
        ns.update_count = 0

        lock = manager.Lock()

        # Create processes
        counters = [
            multiprocessing.Process(target=counter_process, args=(ns, lock))
            for _ in range(4)
        ]

        status_proc = multiprocessing.Process(
            target=status_process, args=(ns, lock)
        )

        # Start all
        for c in counters:
            c.start()
        status_proc.start()

        # Wait for all
        for c in counters:
            c.join()
        status_proc.join()

        # Show results
        print(f"Final counter: {ns.counter}")  # Should be 4000
        print(f"Final status: {ns.status}")
        print(f"Status updates: {ns.update_count}")
```

#### Example 3: Shared List with Aggregation

```python
import multiprocessing
import time
import random

def data_collector(shared_list, collector_id, num_samples):
    """Collect data samples and add to shared list"""
    for i in range(num_samples):
        sample = {
            'collector': collector_id,
            'timestamp': time.time(),
            'value': random.gauss(100, 15)  # Normal distribution
        }
        shared_list.append(sample)
        time.sleep(random.uniform(0.05, 0.15))

    print(f"[Collector {collector_id}] Collected {num_samples} samples")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    with multiprocessing.Manager() as manager:
        shared_list = manager.list()

        # Start collectors
        collectors = []
        for i in range(3):
            p = multiprocessing.Process(
                target=data_collector,
                args=(shared_list, i, 10)
            )
            collectors.append(p)
            p.start()

        # Wait for all
        for p in collectors:
            p.join()

        # Analyze collected data
        data = list(shared_list)  # Convert to regular list

        print(f"\nTotal samples collected: {len(data)}")

        # Calculate statistics per collector
        for cid in range(3):
            samples = [s['value'] for s in data if s['collector'] == cid]
            avg = sum(samples) / len(samples) if samples else 0
            print(f"Collector {cid}: {len(samples)} samples, avg={avg:.2f}")

        # Overall statistics
        all_values = [s['value'] for s in data]
        print(f"\nOverall average: {sum(all_values)/len(all_values):.2f}")
        print(f"Overall min: {min(all_values):.2f}")
        print(f"Overall max: {max(all_values):.2f}")
```

diagrams.title: Manager proxies
diagrams.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  w1["Worker 1: d['a'] = 1"] -->|"proxy call"| srv["Manager server process — owns the real dict"]
  w2["Worker 2: d.get('a')"] -->|"proxy call"| srv
  srv -->|"pickled reply"| w2
diagrams.explain: A `Manager().dict()` is not shared memory: each worker holds a **proxy**, and every access is a message to the manager's server process. That makes managers flexible (any type, even across machines) but slow on a hot path. Note that mutating a nested object returned by a proxy changes only a local copy.

sections.title: 6.5 Shared Memory (Value and Array)
sections.body:
**What this code covers**

- Increment shared counter
- Compute values for a range of the array
- Worker that modifies shared numpy array
- Create shared value and lock
- Compute some expensive function
- No lock needed if each process writes to different indices
- Split work among processes
- Attach to existing shared memory

**Defines:** `increment_counter()`, `compute_range()`, `worker()`

### Visual Explanation


### Code Examples

#### Example 1: Shared Counter with Value

```python
import multiprocessing
import time

def increment_counter(counter, lock, process_id, iterations):
    """Increment shared counter"""
    for _ in range(iterations):
        with lock:
            counter.value += 1
    print(f"[Process {process_id}] Done incrementing")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Create shared value and lock
    counter = multiprocessing.Value('i', 0)  # 'i' = signed int
    lock = multiprocessing.Lock()

    # Create processes
    num_processes = 4
    iterations = 10000

    processes = []
    for i in range(num_processes):
        p = multiprocessing.Process(
            target=increment_counter,
            args=(counter, lock, i, iterations)
        )
        processes.append(p)

    start = time.time()

    # Start all
    for p in processes:
        p.start()

    # Wait for all
    for p in processes:
        p.join()

    elapsed = time.time() - start

    print(f"\nExpected: {num_processes * iterations}")
    print(f"Actual: {counter.value}")
    print(f"Time: {elapsed:.3f}s")
```

#### Example 2: Shared Array for Parallel Computation

```python
import multiprocessing
import math
import time

def compute_range(shared_array, start_idx, end_idx, lock):
    """Compute values for a range of the array"""
    for i in range(start_idx, end_idx):
        # Compute some expensive function
        value = math.sin(i * 0.01) * math.cos(i * 0.02)

        # No lock needed if each process writes to different indices
        shared_array[i] = value

if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Create shared array
    size = 100000
    shared_array = multiprocessing.Array('d', size)  # 'd' = double

    # Split work among processes
    num_processes = multiprocessing.cpu_count()
    chunk_size = size // num_processes

    lock = multiprocessing.Lock()  # Not really needed here

    processes = []
    start_time = time.time()

    for i in range(num_processes):
        start_idx = i * chunk_size
        end_idx = start_idx + chunk_size if i < num_processes - 1 else size

        p = multiprocessing.Process(
            target=compute_range,
            args=(shared_array, start_idx, end_idx, lock)
        )
        processes.append(p)
        p.start()

    for p in processes:
        p.join()

    elapsed = time.time() - start_time

    # Verify results
    print(f"Computed {size} values in {elapsed:.3f}s using {num_processes} processes")
    print(f"First 5 values: {shared_array[:5]}")
    print(f"Last 5 values: {shared_array[-5:]}")

    # Compare with sequential
    start_time = time.time()
    sequential = [math.sin(i * 0.01) * math.cos(i * 0.02) for i in range(size)]
    seq_elapsed = time.time() - start_time

    print(f"\nSequential time: {seq_elapsed:.3f}s")
    print(f"Speedup: {seq_elapsed/elapsed:.2f}x")
```

#### Example 3: Python 3.8+ shared_memory Module

```python
import multiprocessing
from multiprocessing import shared_memory
import numpy as np
import time

def worker(shm_name, shape, dtype, start_row, end_row):
    """Worker that modifies shared numpy array"""
    # Attach to existing shared memory
    existing_shm = shared_memory.SharedMemory(name=shm_name)

    # Create numpy array backed by shared memory
    arr = np.ndarray(shape, dtype=dtype, buffer=existing_shm.buf)

    # Modify our portion
    for i in range(start_row, end_row):
        arr[i] = np.arange(shape[1]) * (i + 1)

    # Cleanup (close but don't unlink - parent will do that)
    existing_shm.close()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Create shared memory and numpy array
    shape = (1000, 1000)
    dtype = np.float64

    # Create shared memory block
    shm = shared_memory.SharedMemory(create=True, size=np.prod(shape) * np.dtype(dtype).itemsize)

    # Create numpy array backed by shared memory
    arr = np.ndarray(shape, dtype=dtype, buffer=shm.buf)
    arr.fill(0)  # Initialize

    print(f"Created shared memory: {shm.name}")
    print(f"Array shape: {arr.shape}, dtype: {arr.dtype}")

    # Split work
    num_workers = 4
    rows_per_worker = shape[0] // num_workers

    processes = []
    start_time = time.time()

    for i in range(num_workers):
        start_row = i * rows_per_worker
        end_row = start_row + rows_per_worker if i < num_workers - 1 else shape[0]

        p = multiprocessing.Process(
            target=worker,
            args=(shm.name, shape, dtype, start_row, end_row)
        )
        processes.append(p)
        p.start()

    for p in processes:
        p.join()

    elapsed = time.time() - start_time

    print(f"Processed {shape[0]}x{shape[1]} array in {elapsed:.3f}s")
    print(f"Sample values: arr[0,:5]={arr[0,:5]}, arr[500,:5]={arr[500,:5]}")

    # Cleanup
    shm.close()
    shm.unlink()  # Free the shared memory
    print("Shared memory released")
```

diagrams.title: Shared Value with its lock
diagrams.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  v[("Value('i', 0) in shared memory")]
  p1["Process 1"] -->|"with v.get_lock(): v.value += 1"| v
  p2["Process 2"] -->|"with v.get_lock(): v.value += 1"| v
diagrams.explain: `Value` and `Array` place C types in memory that all processes map, so there is no pickling. `+=` is still a read-modify-write, so wrap it in `get_lock()` — the same race seen with threads exists between processes.

sections.title: Pitfalls & Gotchas
sections.body:
### Manager Gotcha: Nested Mutations

```python
import multiprocessing

def modify_nested(shared_dict):
    """This WON'T work as expected!"""
    # Direct modification of nested object
    shared_dict['nested']['value'] = 100  # DOESN'T SYNC!

    # You need to reassign the whole nested object:
    nested = shared_dict['nested']
    nested['value'] = 100
    shared_dict['nested'] = nested  # This syncs!

if __name__ == "__main__":
    with multiprocessing.Manager() as manager:
        d = manager.dict()
        d['nested'] = {'value': 0}

        # Nested mutation - broken!
        d['nested']['value'] = 50
        print(f"After nested mutation: {d['nested']}")  # Still 0!

        # Proper way
        nested = d['nested']
        nested['value'] = 50
        d['nested'] = nested
        print(f"After proper update: {d['nested']}")  # Now 50!
```

### Other Pitfalls

- **Queue size**: Default is unlimited, can cause memory issues
- **Pipe blocking**: recv() blocks forever if sender doesn't send
- **Manager overhead**: Very slow compared to shared memory
- **Forgetting to close**: Pipes and queues should be properly closed

sections.title: Performance Notes
sections.body:
| Method        | Relative Speed | Use Case                       |
| ------------- | -------------- | ------------------------------ |
| Value/Array   | Fastest        | Fixed-size numeric data        |
| shared_memory | Very Fast      | Large numpy arrays             |
| Pipe          | Fast           | Two-process communication      |
| SimpleQueue   | Medium         | Simple task distribution       |
| Queue         | Medium         | Full-featured messaging        |
| Manager       | Slowest        | Complex shared data structures |
